title: Experts Ask the Government to Explain What 'Ultraprocessed' Food Means
summary:
What makes a food "ultraprocessed"? Believe it or not, the U.S. government has never given an official answer. Now more than 100 science, medical and food experts want that to change.

On Friday, the experts signed an open letter to the Office of Management and Budget, urging the government to release its first-ever definition of ultraprocessed foods, called UPF for short. The letter said most Americans have heard of UPF and want to avoid them, but few people really understand them.

The effort began in July 2025. In August, health and agriculture officials sent a proposed definition for final review. The foods include sugary cereals, sodas, burgers and store-bought breads. According to media reports, food company bosses stepped in and slowed the release.

The term comes from the NOVA system, created in 2009 by researchers in Brazil. It sorts food into four levels by how much factory processing it goes through. Ultraprocessed foods are broken apart and rebuilt with added colors, flavors and emulsifiers, explained Lindsey Smith Taillie, a nutrition professor at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill.

Studies link eating lots of these foods to heart disease, obesity and Type 2 diabetes. The time for the public to comment on the definition ended on Friday.
why_it_matters: Knowing which foods are ultraprocessed can help you and your family pick snacks and meals that keep your body healthy.

background_read: Many foods in stores are made in factories, where they are changed a lot before they are packed and sold.
The most changed foods are called ultraprocessed: they are broken apart and rebuilt with added colors, flavors and emulsifiers.
Because eating lots of these foods is linked to health problems like heart disease and obesity, experts want one clear official definition so everyone knows exactly which foods count.
